newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary rate hike keeps short-term capital - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Hungary rate hike keeps short-term capital - analyst.

text.p: A recent hike in Hungary's central bank rates partly served to keep short term foreign investment in the country and keep the current account deficit at bay, a Postabank Securities analyst said on Monday.

Attila Torok told a news conference that a category of Hungary's balance of payments defined as 'mistakes and omissions' (MAO) was likely to indicate a rise in short-term speculative investment capital inflow into Hungary since 1995.

"An examination of monthly figures showed a connection between the changes in this column and the temporary slowing and quickening of an interest rate decline," Torok said, adding the category was likely to include speculative capital inflow.
Finance Ministry deputy secretary of state Laszlo Csaba neither confirmed or denied what Torok said.
"Experts argue about MAO but nobody really knows what it is," he said.
"About hot money you can only know that it is hot money when it leaves," he said, adding that Hungary did not have to fear a capital flight as government securities offered attractive real yields.

The amount covered by the quoted column rose from $190 million in 1994 to $1.2 billion in 1995, when Hungary launched a strict austerity programme by which it cut the soaring budget and current account deficits substantially, Torok said.
In 1996, this amount rose further to $1.8 billion, he said, adding that the estimated amount of so-called "hot money" in the country increased to around $1 billion.

Torok said real yields on Hungary's government securities dropped so quickly in the first three months of the year that the NBH had to intervene to prevent an outflow of short-term foreign investments and a fall in domestic savings.
The NBH raised the interest rate on its six-month deposit facility by 0.25 percent to 21 percent three weeks ago, surprising the markets which had expected repo rate cuts.

Torok said Hungary needed foreign hot money to some extent as the working capital inflow is not likely to cover the current account deficit this year, and in case of a capital flight the country's foreign debt could rise.

Postabank Securities expects Hungary's working capital inflow to drop to $1.8 billion this year from $1.9 billion in 1996, while it forecasts $2.1 billion current account deficit for 1997, up from $1.7 billion last year.

Torok said household consumption was likely to rise by up to 2.5 percent in 1997, following a four percent drop in 1996, and in line with that the pace of the rise in household savings would probably slow down in the second half of the year.
In the light of that, the NBH rate hike, which reduced the pace of decline in interest rates, was also aimed at preventing the reversal of a rising trend in household savings, he added.
